goals.title: Teach the sea to build
goals.critique: This is the coast from rounds 1 and 2 again, and it finally has a verb of its own. You don't dig the land yourself. You shape the sea and it builds the land for you, slowly and in ways you can't carry, and a sand bridge to the lighthouse rock is a goal a stranger understands. That indirect control is the first thing in this line that people might name the game after, and the five-tide time-lapse with Truffle crossing is a real clip. The weak part is the loop. Each turn is a long wait for a tide, and real sediment transport is slow, noisy and hard to read, so it can easily feel like a puzzle where you can't see why anything happened. The pitch says you 'read the water' but never says how a player learns that. The road also piles up a GPU shallow-water solver, a transport law, storms, Lumi's sessions and creature settling before anyone checks whether one groyne makes a beach grow in a way that is fun to watch. The pitch sentence is a long list of clauses rather than one plain line.

goals.title: Fold it, throw it
goals.critique: This has the tightest loop of any candidate so far: fold, throw, watch, fold better. Each throw takes seconds and teaches you something, and a race against the creatures' scruffy planes off the cliff is a contest you can clip and send. The weakness is that paper planes and fold-to-fly toys are familiar ground, and the novelty depends entirely on flight coming honestly out of the folded shape. Triangle-panel aerodynamics that make an off-centre crease bank believably, rather than just making it tumble, is unproven and is the whole bet. It is also one small craft at one cliff. Paper is a material you work, but it doesn't build or change the island, so the Minecraft direction is touched rather than carried forward, and there is no reason yet for tomorrow's session to differ from tonight's.
